Describe the space to see the explicit map. The compatibility choice Legacy ambient-node labels restores the previous names without changing beta.

docs.title: Additional computations in the combined flag workspace
docs.text:
Control Concrete behavior Exact evaluations per curve class Two independent exact evaluations by default; one is available but omits the agreement check Parallel workers 1 is serial; 0 requests automatic allocation on this configured path, capped at 12 Hodge diamond Ambient flags or supported ample line-bundle intersections; assumes a smooth regular section Compute quantum matrix Saves exact progress and keeps the matrix symbolic Update spectrum & exponents Requires a completed matrix for the same inputs; reuses it at the selected Novikov point Stop calculation Terminates the running flag job; committed checkpoints remain available for a repeated request

In the combined workspace, omitted Novikov values default to one for analysis. The symbolic matrix remains available. Exact flag exponent analysis requires rational specialized entries; unsupported sectors are reported as unresolved. Neither numerical eigenvalues nor computed exponent classes alone give a rationality verdict.

The standalone gwflags.gui has different specialization behavior: Evaluate y substitutes into the returned matrix and suppresses its separate numerical y=1 display. Its worker value 0 is serial. Do not assume it has the combined workspace's extra buttons.

docs.title: Python and CLI
docs.text:
Unmarked cubic-surface lines:

from gwflags import FlagVariety

X = FlagVariety("A3", [1])
assert X.gw([], beta=(1,), K=[[3]]) == 27

Checkpointed exact flag invariants use the execution wrapper:

from gwflags.execution import configure, gw

X = configure(FlagVariety("A3", [1]),
              checkpoint_directory="flag-checkpoints", evaluations=2)
assert gw(X, [], beta=(1,), K=[[3]]) == 27

Calling X.gw(...) directly retains the original non-staged path. The wrapper above selects staging; configured quantum-matrix blocks also use staging.

A supported non-Fano Hodge example is the plane cubic:

from gwflags.hodge import hodge_report

h = hodge_report("A2", [1], [[3]])
assert h["dimension"] == 1
assert h["hodge_matrix"][0][1] == 1

The returned quantum basis and grading must accompany any analysis:

from gwflags.gui_analysis import matrix_analysis
from gwflags.connection_spectra import connection_report

P2 = FlagVariety("A2", [1])
M, grading, indices = P2.small_quantum_multiplication()
analysis = matrix_analysis(M, unit_index=indices.index(0))
connection = connection_report(M, grading)
assert analysis["cyclic_at_specialization"] is True
assert connection["rank"] == len(indices)

The standalone CLI shares the original flag commands. Put bundle and notation options before the subcommand:

python -m gwflags.cli A3 --keep 1 -K 3 gw --beta 1 --classes ""
python -m gwflags.cli C2 --keep 2 --novikov-convention ambient info

The standalone CLI does not expose the combined application's Hodge and saved-analysis buttons. Use the Python modules or the enhanced workspace for those operations.

docs.title: Reading results and mathematical scope
docs.text:
small_quantum_multiplication returns (matrix, grading, basis_indices). The indices refer to the returned flag's Schubert ordering. For complete intersections this is an ambient sector; Hodge dimensions do not supply missing primitive quantum multiplication.

The original convexity and positive curve-bound conditions remain in force. Changing an input format or a Novikov name does not establish smoothness, an effective cone or ambient completeness.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Keep the workspace directory between runs if you want to resume calculations.
  • Compute a quantum matrix before requesting cached spectrum/exponent analysis.
  • Repeat the same geometry, bundle, evaluation count and naming convention when reusing a completed matrix.
  • Read the reported Hodge support error rather than inferring that every accepted GW bundle supports Hodge reconstruction.
  • Use a separate environment from the preserved original flag distribution: both install the package name gwflags.

See Notation and compatibility and Changes.

docs.title: Checkpoint format compatibility
docs.text:
The prepared build includes the verified 7f167e1 update: faster unmarked shape generation preserves the tested legacy ordering, and large partial-sum fractions are saved as exact tagged hexadecimal integers. Once new tagged values have been written, resume with this updated build; older readers do not understand them.

For the common conventions and concrete result examples, see Input/output. The upcoming release overview explains the differences between the offerings.

docs.title: Preserved original flag software (v1.0.5)
docs.text:
gwflags computes Gromov–Witten invariants and small quantum multiplication for flag varieties G/P and supported complete intersections. The browser interface is the easiest starting point; the Python and CLI interfaces are documented later.

This archived guide describes the preserved v1.0.5 program. Parameter names use ambient nodes; the new notation selector is not available. For installation, use the preserved original v1.0.5 archive.

docs.title: Launch the interface
docs.text:
Follow Installation to install the stable software. Then run:

python -m gwflags.gui --no-browser

Open http://127.0.0.1:8642. The server runs on your computer; stop it with Ctrl-C. Use --port 9000 if the default port is occupied.

docs.title: Fastest path: load an example
docs.text:
1. Choose an item from Preset library.
  2. Read the recommended action and expected result shown below the selector.
  3. Click Describe this space, Compute quantum matrix, or Compute one GW invariant as recommended.
  4. Follow progress in the status and log areas. Large index-1 examples can take several minutes.
  5. After a result appears, use Copy input JSON to save the exact form values (including the selected action), or Download result JSON to save the input together with the complete result for later analysis.

The preset fills every dependent field, so an old β or insertion cannot accidentally remain in a new example.

docs.title: The five core inputs
docs.text:
• Lie algebra: A3, B2, C3, D5, G2, or a product such as A3xA3.
  • Kept simple roots: comma-separated Bourbaki node numbers, for example 1 for projective space or 2 for Gr(2,4) in type A3.
  • Bundle K (optional): leave blank for G/P; enter 3 for O(3), or 1,1;2,2 for two line-bundle summands when the variety has two kept roots (use 1;2 on a Picard-rank-one variety). Semicolons separate summands and commas separate entries within one multidegree. You can also enter taut_quot(X, 2) for a quotient bundle. Use quot(E,F) or Quot(E,F) for a quotient of two bundle expressions; the second argument must be a subbundle of the first. The compact aliases O(1), S(2), and Q(2) are also accepted and are bound to the current variety; use the number of entries required by the kept roots (for example O(1,0) on a two-generator flag). The GUI uses compact text: Python API notation such as [[3]] is not valid in this field.
  • Curve class β: enter one nonnegative integer per kept root, in the order shown in Kept simple roots. A zero-padded vector with one entry per ambient root is also accepted; entries at removed roots must be zero.
  • Insertions: pt, id, or reduced minimal Weyl words separated by |. Copy words printed by Space Info, or click Add beside a basis word.

Evaluate y is optional and applies to quantum matrices only. Variables use ambient node labels (y1, y3, ...), so a variety with kept roots 1,3 uses y1 and y3. Leave it blank for symbolic Novikov variables, or enter assignments such as y1=1,y3=1.

docs.title: Beginner path: direct flags and products
docs.text: For an untwisted direct flag, leave K blank. For example, A2 with kept roots 1 is P²; choose Describe this space first, then choose Compute quantum matrix. A product flag can be entered in the same form: A1xA1, kept roots 1,2, and blank K describes (P¹)².

docs.title: Advanced path: bundle expressions and GW insertions
docs.text:
After Space Info displays the Schubert basis, use its Add controls to build a valid insertion list. This avoids having to know reduced Weyl words in advance. For a homogeneous bundle, first describe the space with the bundle expression, then run the desired matrix or invariant action. taut_quot(X, 2) is directly convex on A4, kept roots 2. The parser also accepts taut_sub(X, 2), but its negative splitting degrees make the supported convex Euler-twisted computation reject that direct input; use dual(taut_sub(X, 2)) for the convex dual bundle.

Goal Algebra Kept roots K β / insertions P² matrix A2 1 (blank) matrix action evaluated P² matrix A2 1 (blank) matrix action with Evaluate y: y1=2 product flag info A1xA1 1,2 (blank) info action 27 lines on a cubic surface A3 1 3 β 1 (or 1,0,0), insertions blank 2875 lines on a quintic A4 1 5 β 1 (or 1,0,0,0), insertions blank Gr(2,4) invariant A3 2 (blank) β 1 (or 0,1,0); 2 1 3 2|1 2|3 2 quotient bundle A4 2 taut_quot(X, 2) describe or matrix action convex dual subbundle A4 2 dual(taut_sub(X, 2)) describe action

docs.title: Reading results
docs.text:
Space Info reports dimension, Fano index, first Chern class, number of curve classes, and the Schubert basis. Use the Add buttons to build insertion lists.

Quantum matrix reports the matrix, grading, characteristic polynomial, and numerical eigenvalues only when all Novikov variables are specialized to one. A custom Evaluate y value is reported separately and does not claim to be the y=1 spectrum.

GW invariant reports the insertion list, the canonical ambient form of β, and the computed number. The degree-zero API path is a classical cup-integral shortcut, including two-point pairings; it is not the definition of an unstable degree-zero GW invariant.

The toolbar above Results keeps the interface reproducible: Copy input JSON copies the current algebra, kept roots, bundle, β, insertions, and options; Download result JSON saves those inputs together with the exact returned matrix, invariant, or space description.

docs.title: Mathematical scope and conventions
docs.text:
The localization formulas use virtual localization on decorated trees. For a complete intersection, the software requires curvewise convexity and computes the Euler-twisted ambient invariant. For the standard geometric interpretation, assume global generation and a regular section with a smooth zero locus of the expected codimension.

The quantum matrix is the flag-ambient operator described above. It is the full small quantum-cohomology operator only when the relevant homology and ambient-completeness hypotheses hold. For complete intersections, the published matrix is an ambient block.

Automatic curve enumeration needs strictly positive first-Chern pairings on the enumerated curve generators. Mixed zero/positive or negative pairings require an explicit Python betas list, unless a supported constructor supplies effective generators with a positive bound. The all-zero Chern class gives a zero multiplication operator. The reported index uses the specified ambient lattice; see the API conventions.

docs.title: Advanced bundle syntax
docs.text: Supported constructors include O(a,...), S(node), Q(node), taut_quot(X, k), taut_sub(X, k), dual(...), osum(...), tensor(...), sym(...), wedge(...), and quot(E,F) (also Quot(E,F)). The compact aliases omit X; the explicit Python spellings remain available. Use the GUI help text for compact line-bundle rows. Nested lists such as [[3]] belong to the Python API only.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Check that kept roots are valid, distinct node numbers in the algebra and in the intended order.
  • β is normally entered in kept-root order; a full ambient vector is accepted only when all removed-root entries are zero.
  • Insertion words must contain integers separated by spaces; separate multiple insertions with |.
  • A catalog entry marked Catalog only has no supported input or computed matrix provided on this site.
  • If a computation is slow, lower the worker count or start with a preset of lower degree.
  • Catalog matrices are rendered by MathJax. If you copy one into a LaTeX document, load amsmath and raise the column limit for the wider matrices:
\usepackage{amsmath}
\setcounter{MaxMatrixCols}{50}

From the repository root, python3 scripts/validate_catalog_tex.py compiles all catalog display blocks in a temporary document.

docs.title: Python and CLI
docs.text:
from gwflags import FlagVariety
X = FlagVariety('A3', [1])
print(X.gw([], beta=(1,), K=[[3]]))       # 27 (kept-root basis)
print(X.gw([], beta=(1, 0, 0), K=[[3]]))  # same, zero-padded form

For the CLI, put bundle options before the subcommand:

python3 -m gwflags.cli A3 --keep 1 -K 3 sqm

docs.title: Bundle combinations: detailed walkthroughs
docs.text: All bundle examples below use the same ambient variety: X = Gr(2,5), entered as algebra A4 with kept roots 2. Begin with Describe this space to confirm the basis and dimension. Then enter one of the following expressions in Bundle K and choose Compute quantum matrix or Describe this space.

docs.title: 1. Quotient bundle
docs.text:
GUI input (both spellings are accepted):

taut_quot(X, 2)
Q(2)

This is the rank-3 tautological quotient bundle. Leave Evaluate y blank for symbolic variables, or use y2=1 for specialization (the kept node is 2). The result summary records the submitted bundle expression, and the matrix is computed using the quotient-bundle twist.

Equivalent Python:

from gwflags import FlagVariety
from gwflags.bundles import taut_quot

X = FlagVariety('A4', [2])
Q = taut_quot(X, 2)
M, grading, basis = X.small_quantum_multiplication(K=Q)

docs.title: 2. Quotient of two bundle expressions
docs.text:
Use quot(E,F) (or the capitalized spelling Quot(E,F)) when F is a subbundle of E:

quot(osum(S(2),Q(2)), S(2))

Here E = S(2) ⊕ Q(2) is a direct sum, and quotienting by its first summand gives the rank-3 bundle Q(2). The tautological exact sequence 0 → S(2) → O⁵ → Q(2) → 0 gives the same class in K-theory as O⁵, but does not identify this direct sum with a trivial vector bundle. The software checks the fiber-weight multisets with multiplicity at every fixed point (equivalent type-A characters are compared after removing the torus-trivial trace direction). Different varieties or a missing weight produce a clear validation error.

Weight containment is a necessary consistency check; it does not construct a subbundle embedding or determine arbitrary extension data. The caller must supply a genuine quotient with supported invariant-curve restrictions.

Equivalent Python:

from gwflags.bundles import osum, quot, taut_sub, taut_quot
E = osum(taut_sub(X, 2), taut_quot(X, 2))
F = taut_sub(X, 2)
K = quot(E, F)
assert K.rank == 3

docs.title: 3. Dual of the tautological subbundle
docs.text:
The subbundle itself is generally not convex for the twisted genus-0 theory. Use its dual instead:

dual(S(2))

The explicit equivalent dual(taut_sub(X, 2)) is also accepted.

Equivalent Python:

from gwflags.bundles import taut_sub, dual
K = dual(taut_sub(X, 2))
M, grading, basis = X.small_quantum_multiplication(K=K)

The GUI accepts the expression, while a direct taut_sub(X, 2) computation may be rejected when its curve splitting degrees are negative.

docs.title: 4. Direct sum of bundles
docs.text:
Use osum to combine summands. This example combines the rank-3 quotient with a line bundle O(1) on this Picard-rank-one Grassmannian:

osum(Q(2), O(1))

The explicit equivalent osum(taut_quot(X, 2), O(X, 1)) is also accepted.

On Gr(2,5) there is one kept node, so O(X, 1) takes one degree. A two-entry constructor such as O(X, 1, 1) belongs on a two-generator product (for example A2xA2, kept roots 1,3). In the compact GUI syntax, separate summands are written as rows such as 1;2.

Python:

from gwflags.bundles import O, osum, taut_quot
K = osum(taut_quot(X, 2), O(X, 1))
print(K.rank)  # 4

docs.title: 5. Tensor product
docs.text:
tensor forms all pairwise sums of fiber weights:

tensor(taut_quot(X, 2), O(X, 1))

Python:

from gwflags.bundles import O, tensor, taut_quot
K = tensor(taut_quot(X, 2), O(X, 1))
print(K.rank)  # 3

docs.title: 6. Symmetric and exterior powers
docs.text:
These constructors derive new bundles from a homogeneous bundle:

sym(2, taut_quot(X, 2))
wedge(2, taut_quot(X, 2))

The first has rank 6 and the second rank 3. In Python:

from gwflags.bundles import taut_quot, sym, wedge
Q = taut_quot(X, 2)
print(sym(2, Q).rank)    # 6
print(wedge(2, Q).rank)  # 3

docs.title: Combining several operations
docs.text:
Expressions can be nested, provided every component is built on the same X:

osum(
  tensor(Q(2), O(1)),
  wedge(2, dual(S(2)))
)

For long expressions, Python is easier to read and debug. The GUI parser only allows the documented constructors and rejects arbitrary Python code.

docs.title: What to check before computing
docs.text:
1. Confirm that every component uses the same algebra and kept nodes.
  2. Use Describe this space first; it reports the resulting bundle rank.
  3. Ensure the combined bundle is curvewise convex for the requested twisted computation. A non-convex bundle is reported as an error rather than being silently accepted.
  4. Start with symbolic y variables. Specialize with Evaluate y only after the symbolic matrix has been assembled.

docs.title: Known archived CLI behavior
docs.text: The preserved v1.0.5 CLI interprets empty insertion text as one unit insertion. Use the Python API or interface for unmarked invariants in that archived version. The prepared corrected build fixes the CLI; no point insertion is required for cubic-surface lines.

docs.title: Input and output conventions
docs.text:
This reference describes the prepared versions gwflags 1.0.6.dev0 and gw-combined 1.1.0.dev1. The preserved v1.0.5 guide describes the archived runtime separately.

Run the cross-engine Python blocks in the complete combined installation, which contains both APIs. The dedicated flag guide provides flag-only examples for the standalone flag installation.

The examples below were generated or checked against the actual prepared sources. Complete example records are available for flags 1.0.6.dev0 and version 1.1.0.dev1 flag, toric and merged modes. Runtimes in those records are incidental and can vary.

docs.title: 1. Select the input model
docs.text:
Item Flag Python API Flag form / CLI Toric Python API Toric form / CLI Ambient target FlagVariety("A3",[1]) Algebra A3; keep 1 projective_space(3), or ToricVariety(rays,cones) Product/preset P3, or explicit fan Node/ray numbering 1-based kept root nodes Same 0-based ray indices Same Cubic defining bundle K=[[3]], or O(X,3) K field 3 or O(3); CLI -K 3 K=[[3]] in the displayed divisor basis Complete intersection 3; CLI --K 3 Unmarked insertions [] Empty field; --classes "" [] Empty field; --classes "" Cubic line beta (1,) in kept-root order 1 (1,1,1,1) as a ray relation 1,1,1,1 One unit insertion [X.schubert(())] id or e [T.one] one

Commas separate entries of a vector. Semicolons separate bundle summands or fan rows. Insertion expressions are separated by |. Flag words use spaces between simple-reflection labels; toric insertions are polynomials such as x0*x1.

The toric interface also accepts newlines between fan/divisor rows. The toric CLI uses semicolon-separated rows. Python lists and explicit ambient arguments belong to Python; a form field does not accept a nested list such as [[3]].

For flags, an ambient-root beta vector is also accepted when it is zero off the kept roots. For toric targets, coordinates in the displayed integral H2 basis are an alternative to the full ray relation. These alternatives must be read from the relevant engine, rather than inferred from the number of displayed parameters.

docs.title: 2. A complete scalar example: 27 cubic-surface lines
docs.text:
Python:

from fractions import Fraction
from gwflags import FlagVariety
from gwtoric import projective_space as toric_projective_space

F = FlagVariety("A3", [1])
T = toric_projective_space(3)

flag_value = F.gw([], beta=(1,), K=[[3]])
toric_value = T.gw([], beta=(1,1,1,1), K=[[3]])

assert flag_value == toric_value == 27
assert isinstance(flag_value, Fraction)
assert isinstance(toric_value, Fraction)

These are unmarked calculations: there are no point insertions.

Flag CLI:

python -m gwflags.cli A3 --keep 1 -K 3 gw --beta 1 --classes ""

Expected stdout:

beta = [1, 0, 0]  # ambient node order
GW invariant = 27

Toric CLI:

python -m gwtoric.cli --preset P3 --K 3 gw --beta 1,1,1,1 --classes ""

Expected stdout:

beta = [1, 1, 1, 1]  (c1.beta = 1 on Z)
GW invariant = 27

In either flag interface, use algebra A3, kept root 1, bundle 3, beta 1 and an empty insertion field. In the toric interface, choose the product P3, set Complete intersection to 3, beta to 1,1,1,1 and leave insertions empty.

An interface serializes the scalar as a string, "27", preserving exact rational spelling. A nonintegral rational uses a fraction string rather than a rounded decimal. Numerical spectra use numerical fields separately.

A verified subset of the standalone flag result is:

{
  "value": "27",
  "insertions": [],
  "beta_input": [1],
  "beta": [1, 0, 0],
  "bundle_rank": 1
}

The toric result instead contains beta [1,1,1,1], c1_beta 1 and Novikov exponent list [1]. The merged flag worker returns value, insertions, canonical beta, evaluation count and its parameter map; it does not promise every standalone flag field. The full subprocess result adds the submitted input and runtime.

These are result examples, not a declaration that every launch mode shares one JSON schema.

docs.title: 3. Quantum matrix outputs
docs.text:
The Python APIs return different third components:

P2_flag = FlagVariety("A2", [1])
P2_toric = toric_projective_space(2)

FM, FG, indices = P2_flag.small_quantum_multiplication()
TM, TG, names = P2_toric.small_quantum_multiplication(cache=False)

assert indices == [0,1,2]
assert names == ["1","x0","x0^2"]
assert [[str(v) for v in row] for row in FM] == [
    ["0","0","3*y1"], ["3","0","0"], ["0","3","0"]
]
assert [[str(v) for v in row] for row in TM] == [
    ["0","0","3*y1"], ["3","0","0"], ["0","3","0"]
]
Output Flag Toric M Matrix of multiplication by c1 in the returned ambient sector Same operator type in its toric ambient basis G Full square diagonal grading matrix in the Python API Full square diagonal grading matrix Third return value Zero-based indices into X.classes and X.class_words() Names of the returned divisor-monomial basis Interface matrix Array of expression strings Array of expression strings Interface grading Diagonal entries, rather than a second displayed full square matrix Diagonal entries Interpretation Input columns, output rows Input columns, output rows

For the P2 example the diagonal grading is [-1,0,1]. The basis labels and parameter maps must accompany a matrix, even when two displayed matrices happen to agree.

A flag basis index is not a root number. A toric basis name is not a curve coordinate. A numerical eigenvalue list is not a substitute for either basis.

docs.title: 4. Parameter names and the two meanings of novikov
docs.text:
Flag names follow the selected convention: paper by default, ambient for the old node names, or compact for consecutive labels in every family.

For C3/keep 3, the default parameter is y1; ambient gives y3. Type A retains node labels by default. Describe the space or read X.novikov_metadata before entering a specialization.

The flag result's novikov field is a metadata object. For example:

{
  "convention": "paper",
  "variables": [{"node": 1, "name": "y1"}],
  "beta_coordinates": "kept-root order or zero-padded ambient roots"
}

The toric scalar-GW result's novikov field is instead the exponent list of the current beta. Its matrix/info results report the Novikov divisor basis. The same field name therefore does not mean the same data type across the two engines.

In toric mode, short K rows use the displayed cohomology divisor basis, while quantum monomials use the reported Novikov divisors. These bases can differ. Effective relation vectors can have negative entries; fallback quantum coordinates can produce Laurent monomials.

docs.title: 5. Symbolic matrices and selected-point analysis
docs.text:
Launch mode Blank evaluation field Custom assignment Standalone flag GUI Returns a symbolic matrix and separately attempts the y=1 numerical spectrum Substitutes into the returned matrix/characteristic polynomial; suppresses that separate numerical spectrum Enhanced combined flag workspace Retains the symbolic matrix; analysis defaults omitted parameters to 1 Retains the symbolic matrix and analyzes the selected exact point Toric workspace Retains the symbolic matrix; analysis defaults omitted parameters to 1 Retains the symbolic matrix and analyzes the selected point

The combined flag Update spectrum & exponents action reuses a completed matrix for matching inputs. The toric Update spectrum & cyclic determinant action reuses its previous matrix; changing the geometry, bundle or curve list requires computing a new one.

Flag exact exponent analysis currently requires rational specialized entries. Unsupported sectors remain unresolved. Connection eigenvalue selection uses K=-M, so its sign differs from multiplication eigenvalues.

Characteristic-polynomial text uses a mathematical symbol named lambda. It is display text, not a Python lambda expression to paste directly into source code.

docs.title: 6. What to retain with a result
docs.text:
For reproducibility, keep:

  • The program version and source revision.
  • Ambient target, bundle, beta or full quantum curve list, and insertion input.
  • Selected flag naming convention, or the toric divisor/Novikov basis.
  • Ordered basis and grading.
  • Symbolic versus specialized matrix status and the exact evaluation point.
  • Curve-list completeness mode and any cutoff or geometric inequalities.
  • Evaluation count where configurable.
  • The exact scalar or matrix expressions, with numerical spectra clearly identified as numerical.

The flag toolbar provides copied input JSON and downloadable result JSON. The toric interface has its own controls; it does not share every flag toolbar action. Its Python API can be used to save a result with the relevant metadata.

Checkpoints are execution state, not a substitute for a reviewed result export. Newly tagged large-fraction checkpoints require the updated reader.

docs.title: 7. Mathematical interpretation
docs.text:
For complete intersections, the returned matrix is the supported ambient operator; a Hodge diamond does not provide a primitive quantum basis. The curve list may be complete under the stated positivity assumptions, conditional on additional geometry, or truncated at an ample degree.

The flag degree-zero API deliberately has a classical cup-integral shortcut, including unstable pairing inputs. The toric degree-zero GW entry path returns the classical integral only for three insertions meeting its dimension check; other insertion counts return zero. These conventions should not be described as identical degree-zero GW definitions.

Use flag 1.0.6.dev0 guide, version 1.1.0.dev1 flag guide, toric guide, and combined guide for the actual controls and supported operations.

docs.title: Software launch — 2026-11-12
docs.text:
This launch brings the flag and toric computations into one documented software collection. Users can choose a geometry, install the appropriate source bundle, and follow a guide whose Python, command-line and interface examples agree with the program.

The prepared versions are gwflags 1.0.6.dev0 and gw-combined 1.1.0.dev1. These published source bundles retain their development version labels. This website launch does not create a new stable software tag. The original v1.0.5 flag runtime remains preserved.

This page is the main change overview. Use Input and output conventions for reproducible formats and Launch preparation for validation scope and publication checks.

docs.title: 1. The software choices
docs.text:
Offering Primary use Distribution and launch Flag program 1.0.6.dev0 Original flag workflow with the prepared notation, CLI and tree-generation corrections gwflags source; python -m gwflags.gui version 1.1.0.dev1 flag engine Flag computations plus checkpointed execution, supported Hodge calculations and connection analysis Complete gw-combined source; standalone flag GUI or enhanced /flag/ workspace version 1.1.0.dev1 toric engine Explicit fans, toric constructors, toric cohomology and supported complete intersections Complete gw-combined source; python -m gwtoric.gui Combined application Choose flag or toric calculations from one local application Complete gw-combined source; python -m gwapp Preserved original flags Reproduce archived calculations using the original runtime and parameter names v1.0.5 runtime and archived guide

There are four current workflows and a historical offering. Individual 1.1.0.dev1 source distributions include the shared execution infrastructure but omit the combined launcher. The combined distribution includes both engines and the enhanced workspaces.

The combined application retains separate geometric inputs and computation engines. It does not translate a flag root system into an arbitrary toric fan or give both geometries one curve-coordinate model.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical and practical differences
docs.text:
Capability Flags 1.0.6.dev0 version 1.1.0.dev1 flags version 1.1.0.dev1 toric engine Ambient description Root system and kept roots Same flag model Rays and maximal cones; product, split projective-bundle and blow-up constructors Cohomology classes Schubert classes Same flag classes Divisor polynomials modulo fan relations Curve coordinates Nonnegative kept-root coroot degrees Same flag coordinates Integral ray relations or displayed H2 basis; negative relation entries are allowed Twisting bundles Supported convex homogeneous bundles, including tautological constructions and operations Retains that bundle API Sums of supported nontrivial nef line bundles Quantum API result Matrix, grading, Schubert basis indices Same flag result convention Matrix, grading, basis names General runtime Hodge module No Ambient flags and supported ample line-bundle intersections Ambient toric diamonds; supported ample Fano CIs in dimensions 3–5 Durable flag progress Original execution path Available through the execution wrapper and enhanced workspace Separate toric execution/checkpoint infrastructure Exact connection analysis Existing spectrum tools Added supported exact cyclicity and exponent analysis Toric connection/spectrum tools with their own supported cases

version 1.1.0.dev1 flag software builds directly on the flag 1.0.x implementation. The differences concern execution and analysis as well as the added toric geometry. The exact genus-zero localization framework and existing supported bundle semantics remain the reference for the flag calculations.

All complete-intersection quantum matrices must be interpreted on their returned ambient sector. Computing a full Hodge diamond does not construct the missing primitive quantum multiplication. Automatic curve lists also have a scope: a conditional Mori search or degree cutoff must not be presented as an unconditional complete quantum operator.

docs.title: 3. Parameter names now follow the documented presentation
docs.text:
The default flag convention is called paper:

  • Type A examples retain ambient node names. A4 with keep 2 uses y2; A2xA4 with keep 1,3 uses y1 and y3.
  • Other families use consecutive parameters in entered kept-root order. C3/keep 3, G2/keep 2 and D5/keep 4 therefore use y1.
  • Mixed-family targets use the same consecutive rule; the explicit returned map is authoritative.

The compatibility convention ambient preserves the previous names. Compact requests consecutive names in every family. The choice is available through the Python constructor, the flag CLI and the flag interface.

from gwflags import FlagVariety

paper = FlagVariety("C2", [2])
legacy = FlagVariety("C2", [2], novikov_convention="ambient")
assert paper.novikov_names == ("y1",)
assert legacy.novikov_names == ("y2",)

This is a parameter relabeling. It preserves beta coordinates, exact coefficients, basis ordering and grading. Results record the selected convention and node-to-parameter map. Existing catalog matrices retain their original labels; use ambient when comparing with those archives.

Toric parameter names are retained. They follow the reported Novikov divisor basis, which can differ from the cohomology divisor basis used by short K rows.

docs.title: 4. Empty CLI insertions now mean no insertions
docs.text:
A blank insertion list is valid. The unmarked cubic-surface line invariant is 27; it needs no point insertion.

The Python API and original flag interface already behaved correctly. The old flag CLI interpreted empty text as a unit insertion. Both prepared flag CLIs now return an empty list for blank text, matching Python and the interface.

python -m gwflags.cli A3 --keep 1 -K 3 gw --beta 1 --classes ""

The result is 27. The corresponding unmarked quintic call returns 2875. An explicit id/e in flag mode, or one in toric mode, still denotes a unit insertion. The preserved v1.0.5 CLI retains its historical behavior and is identified accordingly in the archived guide.

docs.title: 5. Faster unmarked tree generation
docs.text:
The prepared flag programs incorporate the generator from version 1.1.0.dev1 upstream revision 7f167e1. It enumerates rooted shapes, groups equivalent free shapes using AHU, and then selects the legacy lexicographic representatives.

Independent checks established exact representative edges, vertex labels and ordering through six edges. Existing checkpoint tree numbers remain compatible in the tested range. This update improves graph generation while retaining the localization contributions and marking conventions.

The six-vertex cold-generation check took approximately 2.11 seconds with the original generator and 0.011 seconds with the new generator on the verification host. This measures that generator case, not every complete computation.

docs.title: 6. Exact large-fraction checkpoints
docs.text:
The enhanced flag execution path saves exact intermediate fractions. Very large numerators or denominators could make the old decimal writer exceed Python's integer-to-string conversion limit.

The new writer stores large values as tagged hexadecimal numerator/denominator integers. Exact signs and rational values are preserved, and ordinary legacy decimal checkpoints remain readable. The interpreter's global conversion limit is left unchanged.

An old completed checkpoint was resumed with marking evaluation disabled, confirming reuse of its saved sums. Newly tagged values require the updated reader; keep the corresponding updated software with an active workspace.

Flag 1.0.x execution path does not use this staged writer. The storage change belongs to version 1.1.0.dev1 enhanced flag/combined execution.

docs.title: 7. Clearer interfaces and analysis
docs.text:
The standalone flag interface now exposes the parameter convention and displays bundle rank. Its worker help correctly identifies 0 or 1 as serial; the configured combined flag path uses 0 for automatic allocation, capped at 12. Quotient help distinguishes a fiber-weight consistency check from a justified geometric subbundle embedding.

The quartic-threefold preset now recommends describing the space rather than carrying a misleading unmarked benchmark hint.

The enhanced flag workspace adds Hodge, saved-progress, cancellation and spectrum/exponent controls. Its completed-matrix cache distinguishes parameter conventions. Spectrum analysis works at the selected exact Novikov point while preserving the symbolic matrix; omitted values default to one.

The standalone flag GUI substitutes a custom Evaluate y assignment into the returned matrix and suppresses its separate numerical y=1 spectrum. The toric and combined analysis workflows retain their symbolic matrices. These differences are documented rather than hidden behind one generic instruction.

docs.title: 8. Validation and launch status
docs.text:
After the upstream execution update:

Verification Outcome Flag 1.0.6.dev0 suite 74 passed; one socket-dependent HTTP test excluded Flag 1.1.0.dev1 suite 74 passed; one socket-dependent HTTP test excluded Toric regression checks 133 passed Toric Hodge/spectrum tests 19 passed Prepared combined worker/routing/subprocess checks 19 passed Independent tree and fraction checks 27 passed, plus the old-to-new checkpoint reuse check

Fresh legacy-label matrices were compared exactly with original-source calculations, including beta lists, bases and gradings. Paper-label results agreed by exact symbolic substitution. Python examples, CLI calls, actual job functions, generated JavaScript and extracted source bundles were checked.

The environment did not permit a live socket server or browser session. Windows, SageMath, a full package-installation/wheel test and a complete MkDocs build were not exercised. Those checks remain part of launch preparation. These results support the tested cases and do not establish correctness for every possible input.

docs.title: 9. Website publication comes before the later redesign
docs.text:
The content preparation retains the current MkDocs/Material structure and adds clear software choices, version-specific installation instructions, separate guides, exact input/output examples, compatibility notes and preserved original downloads.

The later visual redesign is a separate step. The launch content should remain reusable: its conventions, examples, download identities and validation statements should not depend on a particular page layout.

Continue with the software overview, input/output reference, changes, or launch preparation.

docs.title: Publication and validation
docs.text: The 2026-11-12 launch organizes the universal catalogue by dimension and distinguishes the flag and toric methods and publishes versioned source distributions. Flag 1.0.6.dev0 and flag/toric/combined 1.1.0.dev1 remain development builds. Stable v1.0.5 is preserved with its original behavior.

docs.title: Distributed sources
docs.text: Each ZIP contains package metadata, shared runtime dependencies, a launch handbook and a SHA-256 file manifest. The website download manifest identifies the ZIP bytes. Runtime bundles omit private research notes and local verification dependency copies. The two 1.1.0.dev1 individual bundles include shared flag/toric execution infrastructure and omit gwapp; the combined bundle includes all three packages and its JavaScript assets.

docs.title: Verification scope
docs.text:
The mathematical regression review passed both standalone flag suites (74 tests each, one socket-dependent HTTP test excluded locally), 133 toric regressions, 19 toric Hodge/spectrum tests, 27 independent tree/checkpoint checks and 19 merged-worker/routing checks. Guide examples were executed against their corresponding sources. In particular, the cubic-surface count is 27 with no insertions in Python, CLI and the interface request path.

The source review adopts upstream execution commit 7f167e17a35069ac1ff1cefecce2ac8a0be8231c, plus the documented notation and empty-CLI corrections. The new tree generator preserves the old unmarked representatives and ordering in the independently checked range. Tagged exact checkpoint fractions handle large numerators and denominators; ordinary decimal checkpoints remain readable.

GitHub Actions gates website deployment on the package, catalogue, strict documentation and browser checks. Distribution checks install the exact extracted archives in isolated environments and exercise their launchers. A passing Linux pipeline does not establish Windows or SageMath coverage. Local sandbox restrictions prevented live socket tests; worker tests alone are not described as live browser verification.

docs.title: Catalogue publication
docs.text:
The toric data are imported from completed saved records, with source hashes. The import checks dimensions, full divisor-row lengths, zero-based cone indices, matrix indices and duplicate entries. Further exact checks validate symbolic expressions and grading. These checks do not rerun every localization sum or independently certify every geometry and Hodge calculation.

96 fourfold and 72 fivefold matrices are included. Records with unfinished matrix computations are excluded; completed matrices with unresolved connection factors retain their notes. Fivefold records do not receive rationality verdicts. Their one-evaluation or cached two-evaluation provenance is stated on the collection page.

Main changes · Input/output conventions · Installation

docs.title: Notation and compatibility
docs.text:
The prepared flag builds default to Paper notation. Naming is separate from the curve lattice and does not change any localization coefficient.

Target family Default paper labels Example All factors of type A Ambient Bourbaki node labels A4/keep 2 uses y2; A2xA4/keep 1,3 uses y1,y3 Other root-system families Consecutive labels in the entered kept-root order C3/keep 3, G2/keep 2 and D5/keep 4 each use y1

For mixed-family targets not illustrated above, Paper notation follows the second row: consecutive labels in entered kept-root order. Read the returned mapping rather than guessing a variable name.

Choose the convention explicitly in Python:

from gwflags import FlagVariety

X = FlagVariety("C2", [2])
assert X.novikov_names == ("y1",)
assert X.novikov_metadata["variables"] == [{"node":2,"name":"y1"}]

old = FlagVariety("C2", [2], novikov_convention="ambient")
assert old.novikov_names == ("y2",)

The accepted conventions are paper, ambient and compact. Ambient preserves the previous names for every family. Compact uses consecutive kept-root labels for every family, including type A. The CLI exposes --novikov-convention; the flag interface exposes Novikov notation. Results record the selected convention and node-to-variable map.

Flag beta vectors retain their original meanings under all three choices: kept-root order, or an ambient-root vector zero off the kept nodes. Bases and gradings are preserved.

Toric variable names remain unchanged. They follow the reported Novikov divisor basis; short K rows use the displayed cohomology divisor basis. These bases can differ. A beta relation still has one entry per ray and may contain negative entries.

The preserved original v1.0.5 software retains ambient-node labels. It does not have the new selector or constructor option. Use its legacy guide when reproducing archived calculations.

docs.title: How to use version 1.1.0.dev1 toric software
docs.text: This guide describes the prepared development version 1.1.0.dev1. Install the complete bundle as described in Installation. The toric engine imports shared gwflags infrastructure; gwtoric/ alone is not a complete distribution.

docs.title: Launch the interface
docs.text:
python -m gwtoric.gui --no-browser

Open http://127.0.0.1:8643. The same interface is available at http://127.0.0.1:8650/toric/ when using the combined application. Stop a server with Ctrl-C.

docs.title: Fastest path: load an example
docs.text:
1. Choose P2 from Preset library, or use the Product of Pⁿ tab with factor 2.
  2. Click Fan, cohomology & curves to see the basis, divisor generators and curve coordinates.
  3. For one line through two points, enter beta 1,1,1 and insertions pt|pt.
  4. Click Compute invariant. The answer is 1.
  5. To compute multiplication by c1 instead, leave the optional curve list blank and click Compute c1(TX)⋆ matrix. Read the returned curve-list mode.

docs.title: The core inputs
docs.text:
Field Accepted form Rays Integral primitive vectors, with comma-separated coordinates; separate rays by semicolons or newlines Maximal cones Zero-based ray indices, with commas within a cone and semicolons/newlines between cones Complete intersection One nontrivial nef divisor per row, with one coefficient per ray or coefficients on the displayed cohomology divisor basis Curve class beta A relation vector with one entry per ray, or coordinates in the displayed integral H2 basis Insertions Divisor polynomials such as x0*x1, the unit one, or ambient pt; separate insertions by \|

For the fan of P²:

Rays:           1,0;0,1;-1,-1
Maximal cones:  0,1;1,2;0,2

Enter only the contents after each label. The fan must define a supported smooth projective toric variety.

For P³, K=3 describes a cubic surface. In the One GW invariant area, beta 1,1,1,1 and empty insertions return 27. No point insertion is used.

Different line-bundle summands use different rows: 2;3 gives O(2) plus O(3) on projective space. A divisor with negative ray coefficients can still be nef; the program checks its degrees on invariant curves. Trivial and nonnef defining divisors are rejected.

The Projective bundle tab accepts one divisor per summand of the ambient split bundle. These summands describe the projective-bundle target and are distinct from the later Complete intersection field.

docs.title: Novikov coordinates and spectrum controls
docs.text:
Describe the space first. The displayed cohomology divisor basis used by short K rows can differ from the chosen nef Novikov basis. Variables y1,y2,... follow the reported Novikov divisors, not the raw ray numbers.

Negative entries of an effective beta relation are permitted. If no nef integral Novikov basis is found, the fallback coordinates can give Laurent monomials. Do not replace this with a nonnegativity test on all ray entries.

Novikov point for spectrum & cyclic determinant analyzes the symbolic matrix at selected values; omitted variables equal one. Fractions, decimals, sqrt(...) and I are accepted. The symbolic matrix is retained. The optional eigenvalue selection refers to K=-c1⋆, including its sign. The interface reports unsupported factors without giving a rationality verdict.

Update spectrum & cyclic determinant reuses the previous matrix. After changing the target, K or curve list, compute a new matrix first.

docs.title: Curve-list scope
docs.text:
The result reports whether the automatic calculation uses positive ambient bounds, a conditional Mori search, automatically suggested Mori inequalities, or an ample-degree cutoff.

A cutoff matrix has exact coefficients within its selected region; it is not a complete infinite quantum series. A sampled check of suggested inequalities is evidence, not a proof of the target's Mori cone. User-supplied inequalities must hold on every target curve.

Stop the running computation requests cancellation. It is separate from closing the browser. Durability depends on the selected execution/checkpoint path; do not assume every standalone toric GUI job has the combined flag worker's completed-matrix storage.

docs.title: Python and CLI
docs.text:
from gwtoric import projective_space

P2 = projective_space(2)
assert P2.gw([P2.pt, P2.pt], beta=(1,1,1)) == 1
M, grading, names = P2.small_quantum_multiplication(cache=False)
assert len(M) == len(names) == 3

P3 = projective_space(3)
assert P3.gw([], beta=(1,1,1,1), K=[[3]]) == 27

The toric API returns basis names, rather than the flag API's Schubert indices.

An explicit fan and supported Hodge data:

from gwtoric import ToricVariety

P2 = ToricVariety([(1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1)], [(0,1),(1,2),(0,2)])
assert P2.divisor([3]) == P2.divisor([3,0,0])

P4 = projective_space(4)
assert P4.hodge_report([[3]])["hodge"][1][2] == 5

CLI rows use semicolons. Put ambient and K options before the subcommand:

python -m gwtoric.cli --preset P2 gw --beta 1,1,1 --classes "pt|pt"
python -m gwtoric.cli --preset P3 --K 3 gw --beta 1,1,1,1 --classes ""
python -m gwtoric.cli --preset P2 sqm --workers 1

docs.title: Reading results and mathematical scope
docs.text:
The matrix describes c1 multiplication on the returned ambient sector for complete intersections. Retain its basis, grading, Novikov divisors, curve list and completeness mode.

Ambient toric Hodge diamonds come from the fan. Full CI Hodge support currently requires dimensions 3–5 and the implemented ampleness/Fano certificates; separate Chern-number calculations have a wider supported scope. A supported GW input does not guarantee a supported full Hodge calculation.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Ray indices start at zero; flag root indices start at one.
  • Use the displayed H2 basis for short beta vectors, and the displayed divisor basis for short K vectors.
  • The ambient point class can restrict to zero on a lower-dimensional complete intersection.
  • Leave insertions empty for an unmarked invariant; one means one marked unit insertion.
  • Inspect warnings about truncation or Mori assumptions before treating a matrix as complete.

See Notation and compatibility and Changes.

For the common conventions and concrete result examples, see Input/output. The upcoming release overview explains the differences between the offerings.

docs.title: Toric methods and conventions
docs.text: Let \(Y=X_\Sigma\) be a supported smooth projective toric variety. The rays \(v_\rho\in N\) and maximal cones of \(\Sigma\) determine the target. The order of the rays is part of the input: each cone contains zero-based indices into that list.

docs.title: Divisors and complete intersections
docs.text:
Write \(D_\rho\) for the invariant divisors. Over the rationals, the Chow ring is the polynomial ring in these classes modulo the linear relations \(\sum_\rho\langle m,v_\rho\rangle D_\rho=0\) and Stanley–Reisner monomials for sets of rays not lying in a cone.

A defining row of K represents a divisor \(L_a=\sum_\rho k_{a\rho}D_\rho\); a full row has one coefficient per ray. Short rows instead use the displayed cohomology divisor basis. These are different from the chosen Novikov divisor coordinates. Negative coefficients in a full row do not by themselves imply non-nefness: degrees on invariant curves determine the supported nefness check.

For a regular section of \(E=\bigoplus_a L_a\), assume the zero locus \(X\subset Y\) is smooth and the supported Euler-twisted localization hypotheses hold. Then [ \dim X=\dim Y-\operatorname{rank}E,\qquad c_1(TX)=\left(\sum_\rho D_\rho-\sum_a L_a\right)|_X. ] The interface rejects trivial and non-nef defining summands. A software check of restriction degrees does not certify smoothness of a chosen section.

docs.title: Curves and Novikov variables
docs.text:
A curve is represented by an integral relation \(\beta=(b_\rho)\) satisfying \(\sum_\rho b_\rho v_\rho=0\). The API also accepts coordinates in its reported integral h2_basis. Keep the basis and ray order with the calculation. Effective relations may have negative entries.

The chosen novikov_divisors \(H_j\) define [ y^\beta=\prod_j y_j^{\langle H_j,\beta\rangle}. ] Names y1,y2,... follow that ordered list, not raw ray indices. A fallback without a nef integral basis may produce Laurent monomials. Do not reorder variables from a saved catalogue independently of the basis.

docs.title: Virtual localization and primary invariants
docs.text:
As in the flag calculation, fixed stable maps are indexed by decorated trees. Vertices correspond to fixed points (maximal cones), edges to invariant curves with positive covering degrees, and markings carry evaluation insertions. Tangent weights come from the fan; defining divisors supply the Euler twist.

The software uses exact rational arithmetic and the virtual-localization formula of Graber and Pandharipande, Localization of virtual classes. Auxiliary torus evaluations cancel in the final invariant. Independent evaluations provide a consistency check when enabled; they are not a proof of every implementation formula. New fivefold queue records explicitly used one exact evaluation per curve class, while older cached records may have two-point validation.

For primary insertions, [ \sum_i\operatorname{codim}\alpha_i=\dim X+\langle c_1(TX),\beta\rangle+n-3. ] An empty insertion list means \(n=0\). In particular, a cubic surface in \(\mathbb P^3\) has 27 unmarked degree-one maps; no point insertion is used. In Python: projective_space(3).gw([], beta=(1,1,1,1), K=[[3]]).

docs.title: Quantum multiplication and ambient reduction
docs.text:
The small product is [ \alpha\star\delta=\sum_{\beta,i}y^\beta \langle\alpha,\delta,\phi_i\rangle_{0,3,\beta}\,\phi^i, ] where the dual basis uses the inverse pairing. The complete-intersection pairing is \(g_{ij}=\int_Y\phi_i\phi_j\prod_a L_a\). Selecting a nondegenerate ambient subspace removes its radical; it does not add primitive cohomology.

The returned operator is multiplication by \(c_1(TX)\) on the reported toric-ambient sector. Columns are images of basis vectors: \(Me_j=\sum_iM_{ij}e_i\). Basis entries are divisor-polynomial names; flag API entries instead use Schubert indices. The grading is \(\mathrm{Gr}_{ii}=\operatorname{codim}e_i-\dim X/2\).

docs.title: Automatic curve enumeration
docs.text: The dimension axiom bounds contributing degrees by \(\langle c_1(TX),\beta\rangle\leq\dim X+1\). This is a finite bound only with appropriate positivity and effective-cone information. The result distinguishes positive ambient bounds, conditional Mori searches, suggested inequalities and ample-degree cutoffs. Retain its curve list and completeness mode. A cutoff is exact on its chosen region; a sampled inequality check does not prove a Mori cone.

docs.title: Spectra, connections and Hodge data
docs.text:
Matrices in this toric collection remain symbolic until the displayed eval_y is applied. Unspecified spectrum variables default to one in the software. Saved spectra of \(M\) and connection factors of \(K^F=-M\) have opposite sign conventions; each record states which operator is used. Connection exponents are recorded per factor and per eigenvalue, with multiplicity. Unresolved or noncyclic factors remain explicit.

Fan cohomology gives ambient toric Hodge data. Full complete-intersection Hodge support in the software requires dimensions 3–5 and its implemented positivity certificates; some nef fourfolds instead use attributed literature Hodge numbers. Full Hodge data and ambient quantum matrices have different scopes. Middle \(H^5\) is odd in the fivefold examples and is absent from these even-sector matrices. The automatic irrationality criterion is restricted to dimensions 2–4; the fivefold catalogue assigns no rationality verdict.

docs.title: Reproducibility and sources
docs.text:
Each catalogue entry includes the exact input and sparse symbolic matrix, ordered basis and grading. Published data are transcribed from completed saved records. Validation of those records does not rerun the localization sums. The software guides give Python, CLI and interface syntax.

Fourfold sources: Coates–Kasprzyk–Prince, Four-dimensional Fano toric complete intersections, and Hausen–Laface–Mauz, On smooth Fano fourfolds of Picard number two. Fivefold construction sources and computational caveats accompany their catalogue.
